pass_a_gloss: Matthew-only 'Thy will be done' (Luke silent): pray heaven's accomplished will onto still-earthly selves unto likeness and inheritance. The clause distributes across all three petitions. The heaven-full-of-wicked-powers objection (Eph 6; Isa 34) dissolves two ways: allegorically (heaven=Christ who received the paternal will; earth=church; joined one spirit), and by authority (Mt 28:18, consummation imitation, firstborn's assumed man united to divinity). Deeper: heaven/earth is choice not place — citizenship, treasure, heart, image decide; wicked powers citizen earth; prayer heaven-makes earth until all is heaven, flesh changed to heavenly substance.
pass_b_english: 'Thy will be done, as in heaven, also upon earth.' (Matthew 6:10) Luke, after the 'Thy kingdom come,' passed over these words in silence and goes on: 'Our daily bread give us day by day.' (Ephesians 6:12) So let us examine the words we set first, as lying in Matthew alone, in sequence with what went before. Still being 'on earth,' those who pray conceive that God's 'will' has come to be 'in heaven' among all the dwellers in heaven; and we pray that God's 'will' may come to be in us, who are 'still on earth,' in all things as with them. Which shall happen when we do nothing against his 'will.' And when God's 'will' — 'as in heaven' — is accomplished in us who are 'on earth,' we who are likened to those in the heavens, having borne, like them, 'the image of the heavenly,' (1 Corinthians 15:48–49) shall inherit the 'kingdom of the heavens' (Job 40:19 (LXX)) — we who pray on earth that we, having become 'in heaven,' be likened to them.

But according to Matthew alone, the 'as in heaven and on earth' (Luke 10:18) can be taken in common — so that what is enjoined upon us to say in prayer runs thus: 'Hallowed be thy name' (1 Corinthians 15:50) 'as in heaven and on earth' (1 Corinthians 15:48–50); 'Thy kingdom come' 'as in heaven and on earth' (Job 40:19); 'Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.' (Isaiah 34:5) For God's 'name' has been hallowed among those 'in heaven,' and God's 'kingdom' has stood in them, and God's 'will' has come to be in them — all of which is lacking to us who are 'on earth,' but can come to be ours as we make ourselves worthy to obtain God's hearing concerning all these things.

But someone may ask, saying 'Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth' (1 Corinthians 6:17): how has God's 'will' come to be 'in heaven,' where 'the spiritual hosts of wickedness' are, on account of which God's 'sword shall be drunk' 'in heaven'? And if we so pray that God's 'will' come to be 'on' 'earth' as it is done 'in heaven,' might we unawares be praying that contrary things also remain 'on earth' — since these too come from heaven — with many base things coming to be 'on earth' through the inferior 'spiritual hosts of wickedness' that are 'in the heavenly places'? One who allegorizes heaven, saying it is Christ, and earth the church — for who is so 'a throne' of the Father as Christ? And what 'footstool of God's feet' as the church? — will easily loose the questions, saying each member of the church must so receive the paternal 'will' as Christ received it — who came to do his Father's 'will' and perfected it all. For it is possible, joined to him, to become 'one spirit' with him, thereby receiving the 'will' as one: as it is perfected 'in heaven,' so may it be perfected 'also on earth.' For 'he who is joined to the Lord,' according to Paul, 'is one spirit.' And I suppose this interpretation will prove not contemptible to one who considers it more exactly.

But one who opposes it will set beside it what was said at the end of this Gospel, after the resurrection, by the Lord to the eleven disciples: 'All authority has been given me, as in heaven, also on earth.' (Matthew 28:18) For having authority over those 'in heaven' — he says he has received in addition that 'on earth': those 'in heaven' having been enlightened even before by the Word, and at the 'consummation of the age' those 'on earth' too, through the authority given to the Son of God, imitating the things accomplished 'in heaven,' over which the Savior received authority. As it were, then, through our prayers he wishes to take those discipled to him as co-workers with the Father — that, as the things 'in heaven' are subjected to truth and the Word, so the things 'on earth,' set right through the authority he received 'as in heaven and on earth,' may bring the ruled to a blessed end. And one who calls the Savior heaven and earth the church — 'the firstborn of all creation,' in whom the Father rests as upon a throne, calling him heaven — would find the 'man' whom he put on, made his own by that power through 'humbling himself' and becoming 'obedient unto death,' saying after the resurrection the 'All authority has been given me, as in heaven and on earth' (Colossians 1:15) — the authority 'in heaven,' as of the things indwelling the Only-begotten, received by the man according to the Savior, that he may share it with him, mingled with his divinity and united to him.

But since the second interpretation does not yet loose the difficulties concerning how God's 'will' is 'in heaven,' with the spiritual hosts 'of wickedness' 'in the heavenly places' wrestling against those 'on earth' — from that side it will be possible to loose the question thus: that, as it is not by place but by choice that one 'on earth,' having his 'citizenship in heaven' and treasuring 'in heaven,' with his heart 'in heaven,' bearing 'the image of the heavenly,' is no longer 'of the earth' nor of the 'below' 'world,' but of heaven and of the better, 'heavenly' 'world' beyond this — so too the 'spiritual hosts of wickedness' still lingering 'in the heavenly places,' having their 'citizenship on earth,' plotting against men through what they wrestle, treasuring on earth, bearing 'the image of the earthy' — 'he who is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by the angels' — are not heavenly nor in the heavens, because of their wretched disposition. When, then, it is said 'Thy will be done, as in heaven, also on earth,' (Philippians 2:8) those must not be reckoned to be 'in heaven' at all — having fallen in mind with him who fell 'from heaven' 'like lightning.'

And perhaps, when our Savior commands that we must pray that the Father's 'will' come to be 'as in heaven' 'so also on earth,' he does not at all command that our prayers concern those in the place 'above,' that they be likened to those in the heavenly place. His injunction of prayer is, for one who wishes all things 'on earth' — that is, the worse things, made like to earthly things — to be likened to the better, to all who have 'their citizenship in heaven,' who have all become heaven. For the sinner, wherever he is, is 'earth' — who, unless he repent, shall come to his kindred earth. But he who does God's 'will' and disobeys none of the saving spiritual laws is heaven. Whether, then, we are still 'earth' through sin, let us pray that God's 'will' extend over us too, setting right, as it already reached those before us who are heaven or were heaven; or whether we are reckoned by God no longer earth but heaven already, let us ask that 'on earth' too, as in 'heaven' — I mean, among the worse — God's 'will' be fulfilled, unto the heaven-making, if I may so speak, of earth, so that earth be earth no longer, but all things become heaven. For if God's 'will,' as 'in heaven' in the senses interpreted, come to be 'also on earth,' earth shall not remain earth. As if I spoke more plainly on another example: if God's 'will,' as it has come to be upon the temperate, so come to be also upon the intemperate, the intemperate shall be temperate; or as God's 'will' has come to be upon the righteous, if it so come to be also upon the unrighteous, the unrighteous shall be righteous. That is why, if God's 'will,' as it has come to be 'in heaven,' come to be 'also on earth,' we shall all be heaven — with the unprofitable flesh and its kindred blood unable to inherit 'God's kingdom,' but to be said to inherit if they 'change from flesh and earth and dust and blood to the heavenly substance.' (Philippians 3:20)
